cards.front: How does amphotericin B kill fungi?
cards.back: It binds ergosterol in the fungal membrane. Several molecules line up to form a pore; ions and small water-soluble molecules then leak out, so the cell dies.

cards.front: Why is amphotericin B so toxic to the patient even though it targets fungi?
cards.back: Human cell membranes contain cholesterol, which resembles ergosterol. Amphotericin B binds cholesterol too, though with lower affinity, so its selectivity is poor. It is among the most toxic systemic antibiotics, although it is the least toxic of the polyenes.

cards.front: What is the acute infusion reaction to amphotericin B and how is it managed?
cards.back: Chills, fever, body aches, nausea, vomiting and breathlessness for 2 to 5 hours, probably from cytokine release (IL-1, TNF). Raise the dose gradually after a test dose. Hydrocortisone given with the infusion can blunt it, and it usually lessens with continued use. Thrombophlebitis of the vein can occur.

cards.front: What is the most important long-term toxicity of conventional amphotericin B?
cards.back: Dose-related nephrotoxicity: fall in GFR, azotaemia, hypokalaemia, renal tubular acidosis and loss of urine-concentrating ability. It recovers slowly and often incompletely after stopping. Anaemia from marrow depression is common but largely reversible.

cards.front: Short note: Amphotericin B formulations

points: Polyene from Streptomyces nodosus
Gold standard for most systemic mycoses
Fungicidal at high concentration, fungistatic at low
Powder with deoxycholate, dispersed in glucose (not saline) before IV use
Test dose first, then slow infusion, titrated up toward about 0.7 mg/kg/day
Total course often 3 to 4 g over 2 to 3 months
Most toxic formulation
Lower infusion reaction and nephrotoxicity, less anaemia
Can be infused faster
Preferred for empirical febrile neutropenia, severe deep mycosis and kala-azar
Much costlier

cards.front: Mucormycosis: which drug is first choice and which is the salvage option?
cards.back: Intravenous amphotericin B is the treatment of choice. Fluconazole and voriconazole have no useful activity against Mucorales. Posaconazole is active against some of them and is kept for salvage (KDT). GG14 adds isavuconazole, which covers most Mucorales and is approved for invasive mucormycosis.

cards.front: Cryptococcal meningitis: which two drugs are combined and why?
cards.back: Amphotericin B with flucytosine, which GG14 calls the gold standard for induction; adding flucytosine improves survival compared with amphotericin B alone. Flucytosine acts synergistically because amphotericin B helps it enter the fungus, so the amphotericin dose can be reduced. Flucytosine is kept to about the first two weeks because of marrow toxicity. GG14 also notes that 2 weeks of fluconazole plus flucytosine was as effective for induction as 1 week of amphotericin B plus flucytosine.

cards.front: Which fungal enzyme do echinocandins inhibit, and why are they less toxic than amphotericin B?
cards.back: Beta-1,3-glucan synthase, so beta-1,3-glucan is not made in the fungal cell wall. The wall weakens, the fungus loses osmotic stability and dies. Human cells have no such wall, so toxicity is low.

cards.front: Caspofungin: route, distribution and main uses
cards.back: Not absorbed orally, so given IV as a freshly made solution. It distributes into tissues but does not enter CSF. Preferred for deep and invasive candidiasis, also used for oesophageal candidiasis and for aspergillosis not responding to other drugs. Well tolerated in neutropenic patients with fever.

cards.front: What is the mechanism of azole antifungals and why are triazoles less toxic than imidazoles?
cards.back: They inhibit fungal lanosterol 14-alpha-demethylase, a cytochrome P450 enzyme, so ergosterol synthesis fails and toxic sterol intermediates build up. Triazoles have lower affinity for mammalian CYP450 and sterol synthesis, so they are less toxic.

cards.front: Short note: Classes of azole antifungals

points: Clotrimazole, miconazole, econazole, oxiconazole
Used for dermatophytes, candidiasis, pityriasis versicolor, otomycosis
Ketoconazole is the exception: also oral, but now rarely used systemically
Fluconazole, itraconazole, voriconazole, posaconazole
Fluconazole and itraconazole largely replaced ketoconazole
Voriconazole and posaconazole are newer, broader agents
Dermatophytes, Candida, most deep mycoses
Mucorales are not covered by most azoles; posaconazole and isavuconazole are the exceptions
Also active against Nocardia and Leishmania
Candida in advanced AIDS and fluconazole-resistant oesophageal candidiasis
Usually due to mutation of the 14-demethylase gene
Many fluconazole-resistant isolates respond to itraconazole or voriconazole

cards.front: Why has oral ketoconazole been largely replaced for systemic use?
cards.back: It suppresses testicular androgen synthesis and displaces testosterone from binding proteins, causing gynaecomastia, loss of libido and oligospermia; at higher doses it suppresses cortisol synthesis and disturbs oestradiol synthesis. GG14 adds that oral use can cause hepatotoxicity and adrenal insufficiency, and that in the US oral ketoconazole is available only with restrictions. Itraconazole and fluconazole avoid the hormonal effects, so ketoconazole is now used mainly topically.

cards.front: Classify the interactions of ketoconazole: acid-dependent absorption, enzyme inducers and CYP inhibition
cards.text: Ketoconazole needs {{gastric acid}} for absorption, so H2 blockers, PPIs and antacids reduce it. {{Rifampin}}, phenytoin and carbamazepine induce its metabolism. It inhibits {{CYP3A4}} and raises levels of drugs such as digoxin, warfarin, cyclosporine and statins.

cards.front: Fluconazole: key pharmacokinetics and why it is the azole of choice for meningitis
cards.back: Water-soluble and about 94% absorbed; food and gastric pH do not change this. Mostly excreted unchanged in urine, half-life 25 to 30 hours. It penetrates brain and CSF well, so it is preferred for cryptococcal and coccidioidal meningitis. Dose reduction is needed in renal impairment.

cards.front: Name two deep mycoses that fluconazole does not treat.
cards.back: Aspergillosis and mucormycosis. It is also inferior to itraconazole for histoplasmosis, blastomycosis and sporotrichosis, and for tinea unguium (nail infection).

cards.front: Itraconazole: how do food and acid affect it, and why is it not used for meningitis?
cards.back: Oral absorption is variable and improved by food and gastric acid, so antacids, H2 blockers and PPIs reduce it. It is highly protein bound with a large volume of distribution, but CSF penetration is poor. It is metabolised by CYP3A4 and its active metabolite is excreted in faeces.

cards.front: Voriconazole: drug of choice for which infections, and what are its main toxicities?
cards.back: Drug of choice for invasive aspergillosis, fluconazole-resistant invasive Candida, Fusarium, and febrile neutropenia not responding to antibacterials. Toxicities: rash, photosensitivity, raised liver enzymes, QTc prolongation; short-lived visual disturbances, especially after IV dosing.

cards.front: Posaconazole: what is its distinctive role?
cards.back: Posaconazole is broad-spectrum and active against some of the fungi causing mucormycosis, where it has been used as salvage therapy. GG14 lists its approval for prophylaxis of candidiasis and aspergillosis in patients with prolonged neutropenia or severe graft-versus-host disease. Because of cost, it is otherwise kept for non-responding aspergillosis and invasive candidiasis. It raises levels of CYP3A4 substrates.

cards.front: Essay: Compare fluconazole, itraconazole, voriconazole and ketoconazole

points: All inhibit fungal lanosterol 14-alpha-demethylase
Triazoles preferred over the imidazole ketoconazole for systemic use
Fluconazole: Candida, cryptococcus, dermatophytes; poor against moulds
Itraconazole: adds some moulds; histoplasmosis, blastomycosis, sporotrichosis
Voriconazole: invasive aspergillosis, fluconazole-resistant Candida
Ketoconazole: now mainly topical
Fluconazole: well absorbed, renal excretion unchanged, good CSF penetration
Itraconazole: variable absorption needing food and acid, poor CSF
Voriconazole: well absorbed, avoid high-fat meal, CYP2C19 and CYP3A4 metabolism
Ketoconazole: hormonal effects, nausea
Itraconazole: dose above 400 mg/day poorly tolerated, hypokalaemia, can worsen LV function
Voriconazole: visual change, QTc prolongation, photosensitivity
Azoles inhibit CYP3A4 to varying degrees
Enzyme inducers such as rifampin, phenytoin and carbamazepine reduce levels
Fluconazole has the fewest interactions among them

cards.front: Classify the first-choice drugs for systemic mycoses
cards.text: Cryptococcal meningitis: first choice {{amphotericin B with flucytosine}}, second choice {{fluconazole}}. Invasive aspergillosis: first choice {{voriconazole}} or amphotericin B. Histoplasmosis: first choice {{itraconazole}} or amphotericin B.

cards.front: Terbinafine: mechanism and why it is called fungicidal
cards.back: It non-competitively inhibits squalene epoxidase, an early enzyme in ergosterol synthesis. Squalene accumulates inside the fungus, which is thought to kill it. The human enzyme is inhibited only at far higher concentrations.

cards.front: Terbinafine: which infections does it treat, and for how long?
cards.back: Topical 1% cream twice daily for tinea pedis, cruris, corporis and pityriasis versicolor, for 2 to 4 weeks. Oral 250 mg daily for onychomycosis, tinea capitis and widespread lesions, for 3 to 6 months or longer. Nail cure about 90%, better than griseofulvin or itraconazole. Oral route is not effective for pityriasis versicolor; it is weaker against candidiasis.

cards.front: Flucytosine: mechanism and why it is never used alone
cards.text: Flucytosine is converted inside fungal cells to {{5-fluorouracil}}, which blocks {{thymidylate synthesis}}. Mammalian cells convert it poorly, so it has {{no}} anticancer use. Resistance develops {{rapidly}} if it is used alone, so it is always given with amphotericin B.

cards.front: How does griseofulvin act on dermatophytes, and why is it fungistatic?
cards.back: It binds polymerised microtubules and disrupts mitosis, so hyphae become multinucleate and stunted. Daughter nuclei fail to separate properly. It is fungistatic, so the newly formed keratin is not invaded, but infected keratin stays infected until shed. It has no action on Candida, deep mycoses or bacteria.

cards.front: Short note: Griseofulvin

points: Poorly water soluble, so absorption is incomplete; better with fatty food and microfine particles
Deposits in keratin-forming tissue and stays for weeks
Mainly metabolised by methylation; excreted in urine
Oral only; ineffective topically
Reserve for extensive tinea, tinea capitis and onychomycosis
Duration depends on keratin turnover: scalp about 4 weeks, palms and soles 6 to 8 weeks, fingernails 6 to 8 months, toenails 10 to 12 months
Headache and GI upset are commonest
Rash, photoallergy and hepatitis need stopping
Induces CYP450: lowers efficacy of oral contraceptives and speeds warfarin metabolism

cards.front: Acyclovir: how does it selectively stop herpes virus replication?
cards.back: A herpes-specific viral thymidine kinase converts acyclovir to its monophosphate; cellular kinases then make the triphosphate. The triphosphate competitively inhibits viral DNA polymerase and is incorporated into viral DNA, ending chain elongation. Infected cells activate it far more than uninfected cells, giving a high therapeutic index. CMV is practically unaffected.

cards.front: Short note: Acyclovir in herpes infections

points: Topical therapy works only if started early in mild cases
Oral or IV therapy for severe or late disease
Suppressive oral therapy reduces recurrences and transmission but does not eliminate them
HSV encephalitis: IV acyclovir is the drug of choice; benefit depends on starting early
Disseminated HSV in immunocompromised patients: IV or oral
Zoster: IV in immunodeficient or severe cases; oral therapy must start early
Postherpetic neuralgia is not prevented
Chickenpox: specific treatment reserved for immunocompromised patients and neonates
Ointment for deep stromal keratitis, where corneal penetration helps
Slower than idoxuridine drops for superficial dendritic ulcers

cards.front: Acyclovir: main toxicity and who is at risk
cards.text: The most important toxicity is a dose-dependent fall in {{GFR}}, especially in patients with {{kidney disease}}; it usually reverses on stopping. High IV doses can cause reversible {{neurotoxicity}} such as tremor, confusion and convulsions. No {{teratogenicity}} has been noted.

cards.front: How do valacyclovir and famciclovir improve on acyclovir?
cards.back: Valacyclovir is a valyl ester prodrug of acyclovir; intestinal peptide transporters raise oral bioavailability to about 55 to 70%, giving roughly three-fold higher acyclovir levels, and it is preferred for zoster. Famciclovir is a prodrug of penciclovir with good oral absorption and a long-lived intracellular active triphosphate; it does not work on acyclovir-resistant strains.

cards.front: Ganciclovir and valganciclovir: main use and key toxicity
cards.back: Most active against CMV. Reserved for severe CMV disease (retinitis, pneumonia, colitis) in immunocompromised patients such as those with AIDS or transplants. Valganciclovir is an oral valyl prodrug with about 60% bioavailability and has largely replaced IV ganciclovir for retinitis, except when vision is threatened. Main toxicity: bone marrow suppression, plus rash, fever and neuropsychiatric effects.

cards.front: Cidofovir: why it can be given weekly, and its main safety rule
cards.back: It is a nucleotide analogue active against most DNA viruses, including acyclovir-resistant HSV and ganciclovir-resistant CMV. Cellular enzymes make the active diphosphate, which persists in infected cells, so weekly dosing works. It is given IV with oral probenecid, which reduces its nephrotoxicity. Dose-related kidney damage means it is contraindicated in kidney disease.

cards.front: Foscarnet: why is it reserved for resistant cases, and what are its toxicities?
cards.back: It is a non-nucleoside phosphonate that inhibits viral DNA polymerase and reverse transcriptase, so it works on acyclovir- and ganciclovir-resistant strains, with minimal viral resistance. Toxicity is high: nephrotoxicity with a diabetes-like tubular defect and acute renal failure, anaemia, phlebitis, and hypocalcaemia causing tremor and convulsions.

cards.front: Idoxuridine and trifluridine: class, use and limitation
cards.text: Both are {{thymidine}} analogues used topically for {{herpes simplex keratitis}}. Trifluridine has low virus selectivity because it also blocks {{host cell kinases}}. Ocular {{irritation}} and lid oedema are common adverse effects.

cards.front: Amantadine: mechanism, and why it is seldom used for influenza now
cards.back: A tricyclic amine that blocks the M2 ion channel of influenza A, preventing uncoating of the viral genome. It has no action on influenza B or the H5N1 and H1N1 strains, and resistance arises through M2 mutation. Now rarely used for influenza; occasionally used for parkinsonism.

cards.front: Oseltamivir: mechanism, and why timing of the first dose matters
cards.back: A sialic acid analogue that inhibits viral neuraminidase, so progeny virions cannot leave the infected cell. It is an ester prodrug converted to oseltamivir carboxylate, about 80% bioavailable. Start within 48 hours of symptoms, because viral replication peaks in the first 2 days. Given within 2 days of exposure it can prevent illness in contacts.

cards.front: Oseltamivir: treatment and prophylaxis doses
cards.text: Treatment is {{75 mg}} orally twice daily for {{5 days}}; prophylaxis is {{75 mg}} once daily. Dose is reduced in {{renal insufficiency}}. Taking it with {{food}} reduces nausea and abdominal pain.

cards.front: Zanamivir and peramivir: how they are given, and the key caution
cards.back: Zanamivir is inhaled as a powder because oral bioavailability is very low; it is kept for oseltamivir-resistant or severe cases. It can cause bronchospasm, so it is contraindicated in asthma. Peramivir is a single IV dose (600 mg) given within 48 hours of onset, cleared by the kidney, and useful when other drugs cannot be given.

cards.front: Ribavirin: uses and toxicity
cards.text: Older hepatitis C therapy combined oral ribavirin with injected {{peginterferon alpha}} (KDT); with direct-acting antivirals it is now only added to some regimens, for example in {{decompensated cirrhosis}} (GG14). Aerosolised ribavirin is used for {{respiratory syncytial virus}} infection. Its major toxicity is dose-related {{haemolytic anaemia}}. It is teratogenic, so contraception is needed during treatment and for {{3 months}} afterwards (KDT).

cards.front: Interferon alpha: mechanism and major adverse effects
cards.back: Host cytokines that signal through JAK-STAT receptors and induce antiviral proteins, which mainly block viral protein synthesis. Given by s.c. or i.m. injection; pegylated forms are given weekly. Adverse effects: flu-like symptoms after each dose, neuropsychiatric effects, neutropenia and thrombocytopenia, thyroid dysfunction, alopecia. Contraindicated in pregnancy, decompensated cirrhosis and autoimmune disease. Katzung notes that oral nucleos(t)ide analogues have greatly reduced interferon use in hepatitis B, and GG14 notes that direct-acting antivirals have replaced interferon-based therapy for hepatitis C.

cards.front: Entecavir: administration and dosing in chronic hepatitis B
cards.text: Entecavir is a {{guanosine}} analogue and is taken on an {{empty stomach}}, since food reduces absorption. The dose is {{0.5 mg}} once daily, or {{1 mg}} once daily if the patient is lamivudine-resistant. Lactic acidosis can occur in {{decompensated cirrhosis}}.

cards.front: Short note: Nucleoside analogues for chronic hepatitis B

points: 300 mg once daily; a first-line drug; dose reduced in renal impairment
Effective even in lamivudine-resistant disease; resistance rare
Watch renal function: creatinine rise is common
Tenofovir alafenamide (TAF) 25 mg daily: as effective as TDF with less loss of bone density and kidney function (GG14)
Current first-line option; faster viral fall than lamivudine
Resistance rare, mainly in lamivudine-resistant patients
Least active of the nucleotide analogues; not first-line
Resistance in about 30% of patients
Nephrotoxic at higher doses
Telbivudine: not first-line; resistance frequent, especially after lamivudine resistance
Lamivudine: no longer first-line for HBV because resistance reaches up to 70% in 1 to 5 years
Do not stop abruptly: flare of hepatitis can follow
Continue nucleos(t)ide therapy until about 6 months after seroconversion
Combinations are not superior; drugs are used sequentially

cards.front: Sofosbuvir: mechanism and main cautions
cards.back: A uridine nucleotide analogue prodrug converted in hepatocytes to its triphosphate, which inhibits the HCV NS5B RNA polymerase and terminates the viral RNA chain. Because NS5B is well conserved, it is active against all genotypes; it is always used in combination, e.g. with daclatasvir, ledipasvir or velpatasvir. It is a P-glycoprotein substrate, so avoid P-gp inducers such as rifampin. Severe bradycardia has been reported with amiodarone. GG14 states that there are now no renal restrictions on sofosbuvir-based therapy, as emerging data show it is safe and effective in renal impairment.

cards.front: Classify the direct-acting HCV drugs by target
cards.text: NS5B polymerase inhibitor: {{sofosbuvir}}. NS3/4A protease inhibitors: {{glecaprevir}}, {{grazoprevir}} and {{voxilaprevir}} (KDT also lists simeprevir). NS5A inhibitors: {{daclatasvir}}, {{ledipasvir}}, {{velpatasvir}}, {{pibrentasvir}} and {{elbasvir}}. All are used in {{combination}}, never alone.

cards.front: Essay: Treatment of chronic hepatitis C

points: Sustained viral response (SVR): KDT defines it as undetectable HCV-RNA 6 months after therapy; newer trials report SVR 12 weeks after therapy (SVR12)
Relapse only about 5% once achieved
Peginterferon alpha plus oral ribavirin
Response about 50 to 80%; long course and poor tolerability
NS5B, NS3/4A and NS5A inhibitors
Used in combination; monotherapy causes resistance
Most patients now have at least a 90% chance of SVR; decompensated cirrhosis responds less well
Pangenotypic: sofosbuvir/velpatasvir for 12 weeks; glecaprevir/pibrentasvir for 8 weeks in treatment-naive patients
Sofosbuvir with daclatasvir or ledipasvir
Ribavirin added in decompensated cirrhosis and some genotype 3 or cirrhotic patients
Glecaprevir/pibrentasvir is a treatment of choice in renal impairment
Many interactions via P-gp and CYP3A4; potent inducers such as rifampin are avoided
Acid suppressants reduce ledipasvir and velpatasvir absorption

cards.front: Which two viral enzymes are the established drug targets in HIV, and what does each do?
cards.back: Reverse transcriptase, which copies viral RNA into proviral DNA, and protease, which cuts the large viral polyprotein into functional proteins. Newer targets include viral fusion with the CD4 cell, the CCR5 co-receptor and integrase, which inserts proviral DNA into the host genome.

cards.front: Zidovudine: mechanism, main toxicity and key interaction
cards.back: A thymidine analogue; after phosphorylation it inhibits HIV reverse transcriptase and terminates the DNA chain. Dose-related anaemia and neutropenia are the main toxicities; myopathy and lactic acidosis are less common. Paracetamol increases its toxicity by competing for glucuronidation. Never used alone.

cards.front: Classify the toxicities of stavudine and didanosine
cards.text: Stavudine causes {{lipodystrophy}}, {{lactic acidosis}} and {{peripheral neuropathy}}, so it is largely avoided. Didanosine's main dose-related toxicity is {{peripheral neuropathy}}, and it does not cause {{myelosuppression}}. Stavudine and zidovudine should not be combined because they compete for the same activation step.

cards.front: Lamivudine: why is it used for both HIV and hepatitis B, and why is it no longer first-line for HBV?
cards.back: It inhibits both HIV reverse transcriptase and HBV DNA polymerase. It is well absorbed, has low systemic toxicity, is mostly excreted unchanged (so usable in hepatic insufficiency) and is an essential part of most first-line HIV triple regimens. For HBV, resistance by point mutation reaches up to about 70% within 1 to 5 years, so it is no longer a first-line HBV drug.

cards.front: Abacavir: main safety issue and what must happen when it occurs
cards.back: A hypersensitivity reaction, potentially fatal, in about 2 to 9% of patients (KDT: 2 to 5%), usually within the first 6 weeks: fever, rash, abdominal pain, GI upset and sometimes respiratory symptoms. Stop immediately and never rechallenge. It is genetically linked to HLA-B*5701, so Katzung advises testing for this allele before starting, and GG14 says abacavir must not be used in carriers. Avoid in patients with cardiovascular risk factors.

cards.front: Tenofovir disoproxil: why is it widely used, and what should be monitored?
cards.back: It is the only nucleotide (not nucleoside) reverse transcriptase inhibitor in common use and is also active against HBV. It is well tolerated, with few GI side effects, and is in preferred first-line WHO regimens. Monitor renal function: creatinine rise is common and acute or chronic kidney injury is possible. Dose 300 mg daily.

cards.front: Emtricitabine: what distinguishes it from lamivudine?
cards.back: A cytidine analogue with a long intracellular half-life of the triphosphate (about 40 hours), so it is dosed once daily. Renally excreted and needs dose adjustment in renal impairment. It is one of the least toxic ARVs and is supplied only as fixed-dose combinations. It must not be combined with lamivudine, and stopping it in HIV-HBV coinfection can cause rebound hepatitis.

cards.front: NNRTIs: mechanism and rules of use
cards.text: NNRTIs bind HIV reverse transcriptase {{non-competitively}} and do not need {{intracellular phosphorylation}}. They act on HIV-1 but not {{HIV-2}}. Resistance appears {{rapidly}} if used alone, so they are always given with two other drugs. Nevirapine and efavirenz show {{cross-resistance}} with each other, but not with NRTIs or PIs.

cards.front: Short note: Efavirenz versus nevirapine

points: Both are enzyme inducers that autoinduce their own metabolism
Nevirapine: 200 mg daily for 2 weeks, then 200 mg twice daily
Efavirenz: no lead-in; long half-life so occasional missed doses are less harmful
Nevirapine: rash (can be severe), fever, transaminase rise; potentially hepatotoxic; avoid in hepatic dysfunction
Efavirenz: headache, dizziness, insomnia, neuropsychiatric effects; gynaecomastia; teratogenicity not confirmed in humans
Rifampin lowers nevirapine levels: switch to efavirenz if TB needs treatment
Efavirenz is metabolised mainly by CYP2B6 and also inhibits CYP3A4
KDT (WHO 2016): efavirenz preferred first-line, including in pregnancy and breastfeeding
Newer texts: dolutegravir is increasingly the preferred starting agent (GG14); efavirenz is an alternative in pregnancy (Katzung16)
Nevirapine is an alternative but avoided with liver disease or rifampin

cards.front: Protease inhibitors: mechanism, and why they act on both new and old infected cells
cards.back: They block the aspartic protease that cleaves the viral polyprotein at the maturation step, so new virions are immature and non-infectious. They do not need intracellular activation, so they work in newly and chronically infected cells. They are not used alone because resistance develops within months.

cards.front: What is ritonavir boosting, and which protease inhibitor is not boosted?
cards.back: Low-dose ritonavir (100 mg) strongly inhibits CYP3A4, raising the partner PI's levels and allowing fewer tablets a day. Nelfinavir is not boosted because it is metabolised mainly by CYP2C19, which ritonavir does not inhibit. Full-dose ritonavir is rarely used as an antiretroviral because of its side effects.

cards.front: Classify the adverse effects of protease inhibitors
cards.text: PIs cause {{lipodystrophy}} (abdominal fat gain, buffalo hump, limb wasting), {{dyslipidaemia}} and {{insulin resistance}}, plus GI intolerance. Indinavir can crystallise in {{urine}} and cause {{nephrolithiasis}}. Atazanavir can cause {{jaundice}} without liver damage by inhibiting glucuronyl transferase.

cards.front: Integrase inhibitors (raltegravir, dolutegravir): action and key interactions
cards.back: They block strand transfer, so proviral DNA is not inserted into the host chromosome. Both act on HIV-1 and HIV-2 with no cross-resistance to other classes; dolutegravir also works against some raltegravir-resistant virus and resistance to it is rare. Dolutegravir (50 mg once daily) is increasingly used as a starting agent, often as a generic once-daily tablet with tenofovir and lamivudine. Adverse points (GG14): weight gain; a small, uncertain neural tube defect signal with use at conception; it inhibits renal OCT2, causing a small reversible creatinine rise and doubling metformin levels. Calcium, magnesium and iron products chelate them and should be staggered. With rifampin, give dolutegravir 50 mg twice daily and raltegravir 800 mg twice daily.

cards.front: Enfuvirtide and maraviroc: where each blocks HIV entry and when each is used
cards.back: Enfuvirtide is a synthetic peptide that binds gp41 and blocks fusion of viral and cell membranes; given s.c. twice daily to multidrug-resistant patients with no other option, and causes painful injection-site nodules. Maraviroc blocks the host CCR5 co-receptor, so it works only on CCR5-tropic virus and tropism must be shown first.

cards.front: Essay: First-line ART for a treatment-naive adult

points: Start ART as soon as HIV is confirmed, whatever the CD4 count (WHO 2016)
Always at least three drugs from at least two classes
Target: HIV-RNA below 50 copies/mL and near-normal CD4 within 6 months
Lifelong therapy, even after viral suppression
Two NRTIs plus one NNRTI
Tenofovir + lamivudine (or emtricitabine) + efavirenz
Efavirenz preferred over nevirapine; etravirine reserved for NNRTI failure
Zidovudine-based regimens with efavirenz or nevirapine
Tenofovir or abacavir with lamivudine plus dolutegravir
Dolutegravir-based regimens favoured where cost allows
Treatment is offered to all infected people regardless of CD4 count
Dolutegravir, often as a once-daily generic tablet with tenofovir and lamivudine, is increasingly the starting agent; dolutegravir + lamivudine is the only approved two-drug first-line regimen
Expected outcome: HIV-RNA below 50 copies/mL within 24 weeks
Monotherapy and three-NRTI regimens
Nevirapine with hepatic dysfunction or rifampin
PI-sparing regimens preferred for treatment-naive patients
Adherence is the main determinant of outcome
If toxicity develops, change the offending drug or regimen; do not reduce doses
Watch for IRIS when treating latent opportunistic infection

cards.front: After failure of first-line ART, what should change and what are the WHO 2016 second-line options?
cards.back: Change the entire failed regimen, not a single drug, and avoid cross-resistant drugs (for example nevirapine for efavirenz, emtricitabine for lamivudine). Use two NRTIs plus one ritonavir-boosted PI. After failure on tenofovir plus lamivudine or emtricitabine, use zidovudine plus lamivudine; after failure on zidovudine or stavudine plus lamivudine, use tenofovir plus lamivudine or emtricitabine. Preferred boosted PIs are atazanavir or lopinavir.

cards.front: PrEP: which drugs are used and who should be offered it?
cards.back: Tenofovir disoproxil 300 mg with emtricitabine 200 mg once daily; KDT cites a meta-analysis showing about a 51% reduction in HIV risk against placebo, and WHO advises offering it to people at high risk (men who have sex with men, sex workers, people who inject drugs, transgender people, and uninfected partners in serodiscordant couples). GG14 adds that tenofovir alafenamide with emtricitabine is also approved, and that long-acting injectable cabotegravir every 8 weeks was more effective than daily oral tenofovir-emtricitabine in prevention trials.

cards.front: Short note: Post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) for HIV

points: High: source symptomatic with high viral load or low CD4 and not on ART; deep or large-bore needle; visible blood on needle; sexual exposure
Low: source on ART or asymptomatic with low viral load and high CD4; superficial or small exposure
None: source HIV-negative; intact skin; urine, sweat, non-bloody saliva
KDT (WHO 2016) preferred: tenofovir + lamivudine (or emtricitabine), plus lopinavir/r
Alternative third drug: atazanavir/r, darunavir/r, efavirenz or raltegravir
Katzung16: dolutegravir is now used for non-occupational PEP; zidovudine is an NRTI option
Nevirapine is not recommended for PEP in adults or in children over 2 years, because of hepatotoxicity
Course is 4 weeks
Minimum two NRTIs, ideally with a third drug of another class

cards.front: PEP: how soon must it start, and what is the regimen after sexual exposure?
cards.back: Start as soon as possible, ideally within 1 to 2 hours. Benefit falls with delay, and it is generally not started beyond 72 hours. After sexual exposure the same regimen as for needle-stick is used; a popular US option is tenofovir plus emtricitabine daily with raltegravir 400 mg twice daily.

cards.front: Essay: Prevention of mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT) of HIV

points: Transmission in utero, during delivery, or by breastfeeding
Highest risk is during the birth process
All HIV-positive women not on ART start standard triple ART
Continue through delivery and into the postnatal period
Benefits the mother's own health too
Tenofovir 300 mg + lamivudine 300 mg + efavirenz 600 mg as one daily tablet
WHO 2016 keeps efavirenz in the preferred first-line regimen for pregnant and breastfeeding women
Dolutegravir, raltegravir and boosted atazanavir or darunavir are among the agents recommended in pregnancy; efavirenz is an alternative
Nevirapine syrup for 6 weeks
Caesarean section advised if HIV-RNA is above 1000 copies/mL near delivery

cards.front: Classify the ARV combinations to avoid
cards.text: Avoid zidovudine with {{stavudine}} (pharmacodynamic antagonism); stavudine with {{didanosine}} (neuropathy and lactic acidosis); lamivudine with {{emtricitabine}} (similar drugs); lamivudine with {{didanosine}} (not additive); tenofovir with {{didanosine}} (lower efficacy).

cards.front: Isavuconazole: spectrum, uses and interactions
cards.back: A triazole with broad activity against most yeasts (Candida, Cryptococcus) and moulds, including Aspergillus and most Mucorales. It is approved for invasive aspergillosis and invasive mucormycosis. It is both a substrate and an inhibitor of CYP3A4: strong inhibitors such as ketoconazole raise its levels several-fold and rifampin lowers them, and it raises midazolam and sirolimus levels. Unlike other azoles it shortens the QTc in a dose-related way.

cards.front: Baloxavir marboxil: mechanism and use
cards.back: An oral prodrug converted to baloxavir acid, which inhibits the influenza cap-dependent endonuclease and so blocks the start of viral mRNA synthesis. It is active against influenza A and B. It is used to treat acute uncomplicated influenza in patients aged 12 years and older who have had symptoms for no more than 2 days, including those at high risk of complications, and for post-exposure prophylaxis after contact with a case.

cards.front: Letermovir: how does it differ from ganciclovir?
cards.back: It inhibits the CMV DNA terminase complex (UL56/UL89), which cleaves and packages newly made viral DNA, rather than the viral DNA polymerase. It is used for prophylaxis of CMV infection and disease in CMV-seropositive adults receiving an allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplant, and it was the first new anti-CMV drug licensed in over 20 years.
